findings.title: Recovery codes held in user storage are never consumed, so they can be replayed
findings.body: isValid for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks whether the submitted code is in the stored list and never removes or marks it as used. The core RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator (lines 80-92) decides when to retire the credential and force regeneration solely from the credential's allCodesUsed() state. For a federated credential that state is rebuilt from the raw stored list by getCredentials (new model, no used-state), so allCodesUsed() can never become true. The result is that a recovery code which logged a user in once keeps working indefinitely, while the local provider consumes codes. Nothing in the core flow writes used-state back to user storage either. The new test performs only one successful login and never attempts a second use, so this goes undetected.

findings.title: Recovery codes are sent to user storage in plaintext while local storage keeps only hashes
findings.body: generatedCodes are the raw codes shown to the user. They are serialized to JSON and passed unhashed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...), so any external user storage provider (LDAP, a custom DB) persists usable bearer login secrets. The local path stores only RS512 hashes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode). A read of the external store therefore yields directly usable recovery codes, and the test provider compares raw strings. Either hash the codes before handing them to user storage (and hash the input on verification) or explicitly document and accept the difference.

findings.title: New recovery-codes test covers only the happy path
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin sets up codes, logs in once with code 0 and stops. It does not check that a wrong code is rejected, that a used code cannot be reused (which the user-storage path currently fails, see the isValid comment), that the stored codes are visible through the account/admin credential APIs (the new getCredentials override is not exercised), or that the local fallback still works when a storage provider does not support recovery codes. The reuse gap in particular is exactly what this test should catch.

findings.title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly null MyUser
findings.body: getMyUser(user) returns null when the user is not in the users map, and getCredentials immediately dereferences myUser.recoveryCodes and myUser.otp with no null check. The sibling methods getDisableableCredentialTypesStream and isConfiguredFor guard against this case, so this one throws NullPointerException where the others return empty results.

findings.title: supportsCredentialType throws NPE for a null type
findings.body: The previous implementation was null-safe (CredentialModel.PASSWORD.equals(null) and isOTPType(null) return false). The new clause credentialType.equals(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE) is evaluated for a null argument and throws NullPointerException instead of logging and returning false. Comparing against the constant (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE.equals(credentialType)) would avoid this.

findings.title: Recovery codes in user storage cannot be disabled or listed as disableable
findings.body: disableCredentialType only handles OTP and logs 'Unsupported' for anything else, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream never includes the recovery type. Admin disable-credential requests for a federated user therefore silently leave the stored recovery codes in place, and the admin API does not offer them as disableable. The local path supports revoking these codes, so the behaviour is inconsistent with the feature being added.

findings.title: userLabel and generatedAt are silently dropped in the user-storage branch
findings.body: The credentialModel passed in carries the user-provided userLabel and the generatedAt timestamp, and the local branch persists them. The user-storage branch builds only a UserCredentialModel from the type and the JSON codes, so these values are discarded. The test provider then stamps createdDate with the current time and has no label. Users who set a label or check creation dates will see different metadata depending on where the codes ended up, without any indication.
